opus-5.5.text:
I think the two ecosystems will evolve quite differently, though they're more connected than people usually assume.

On the closed-source side, I expect consolidation. Pushing the frontier keeps getting more expensive: compute, data, and especially the talent and organizational ability to run very large training efficiently. Each generation raises the bar. So over time you'll probably see only a handful of players, maybe three to five globally, who can consistently sit at the very top. Others will still build closed models, but they'll increasingly focus on specific verticals or products rather than competing head-on for general capability.

Open source is more interesting. The number of participants will stay large, maybe even grow, because the barrier to *using* and *improving* models keeps dropping. Once a strong base model is released, thousands of teams can fine-tune it, distill it, adapt it to new domains, and build agents on top. But the number of organizations that can produce a truly frontier-level open base model will also be small. The pattern is a few strong providers at the foundation and a very wide, vibrant layer on top.

The relationship between the two matters a lot. In the past year or two, the gap between the best open models and the best closed ones has narrowed significantly. When that happens, simply having a closed model is no longer a moat. Value shifts to how fast you can iterate, whether you have a real product with real users generating feedback, and whether you can push capabilities like long-horizon reasoning and agentic tasks that aren't easily replicated.

For a company like ours, the question isn't really "open or closed" as an ideology. It's about where you can create the most value and stay at the technical frontier. Open-sourcing strong models can be a strategic choice. It builds an ecosystem, attracts developers, and shows technical credibility. But only if you keep moving forward, because in this field standing still means falling behind very quickly.

So in short, I expect fewer frontier players overall, open and closed combined, and a much broader ecosystem of builders on top. The winners will be the ones who keep improving the core intelligence while also finding a real product loop.

r001.rationale: The response predicts a handful of top closed-source players and few frontier open-model providers, but says the broader open-source ecosystem will stay large or grow. It does not predict a few players as the endpoint for both ecosystems overall.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the number of players will keep shrinking, and it will shrink faster than most people expect. Training frontier models is a game where the cost of each generation goes up by something like an order of magnitude, and the number of organizations that can afford that, and more importantly that can afford to be wrong a few times, is very small. So on the closed-source side, globally, I'd expect maybe three to five players who are genuinely at the frontier. In China, probably a similar or slightly smaller number. Everyone else will either specialize, go downstream into applications, or quietly stop pretraining their own base models.

Open source is a bit different, but not as different as people think. Open source doesn't really mean there are more model producers. It means the models that do get produced are shared more widely. So you still have a small number of labs, maybe Meta, maybe a few Chinese companies, maybe one or two others, actually training strong open models, and then a very long tail of people fine-tuning and deploying them. The concentration at the top is similar; what changes is who gets to build on top.

The interesting question is whether open models stay close to the frontier or fall further behind. My view is that there will be a gap, and the gap is roughly one generation. Open models catch up to where closed models were a year or so earlier. That gap might not close, because the economics of releasing your very best model for free are hard to justify once the cost is in the billions. But a one-generation gap is still enormously useful for most applications, so the open ecosystem will remain very healthy at the application layer even as the number of base-model trainers consolidates.

So to summarize: fewer and fewer people training foundation models, both open and closed, converging toward a handful. Many more people building on them. The real competition in the long run is not open versus closed; it's who has the capability to keep pushing the frontier, and who can turn that into products people actually use.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that base-model training in both ecosystems will consolidate toward a handful of players, describing a few frontier closed-source labs and a small number of open-model producers.

astra-6.text:
I think both will become more concentrated, but in different ways. For closed-source models, training at the frontier requires a lot of capital, compute, and research talent. So I’d expect a relatively small number of companies to keep competing at that level. There can still be many application companies built on top of them.

With open source, I’d distinguish between the teams producing the base models and the people adapting those models. There may only be a few widely used base-model families, but each can support a large ecosystem of fine-tunes, tools, and specialized applications. So you could see fewer players at the foundation-model layer while participation in the broader ecosystem continues to grow.

I wouldn’t put an exact number on either side. It depends partly on whether new research makes it much cheaper for a small team to produce a competitive model.

r001.rationale: The response expects a small number of closed-source frontier competitors and a few open-source base-model families, but says participation in the broader open-source ecosystem may grow. It does not clearly predict that a few players will be a relatively stable endpoint for both ecosystems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think both will become more concentrated, but in different ways. Training frontier models requires a lot of capital, compute, and a strong research team, so the number of companies that can consistently compete at that level may be relatively small.

For open source, you might have a few widely adopted base models, with many more teams fine-tuning them, building tools, and developing applications. So a small number of model providers can support a very large ecosystem.

For closed source, the question is whether a company has enough differentiation to sustain the investment. That could come from model capability, distribution, or a product that users really value. I don’t think every company needs to train its own foundation model. There will probably be fewer players at the foundation-model layer and many more building on top of it.

r001.rationale: The response predicts greater concentration and fewer foundation model providers, but does not say that a few players will become a relatively stable endpoint for both ecosystems. It also describes many teams participating in the open-source ecosystem.
